newsitem.title: ISRAEL: "Who is a Jew" issue ties up Israel finance chief.
newsitem.headline: "Who is a Jew" issue ties up Israel finance chief.

text.p: Yaacov Neeman, Israel's newly appointed finance minister, said on Wednesday he could not give full attention to his new post for another month because he is also heading a panel on the issue of conversion to Judaism.

"To my great misfortune I have another position in addition to my position at the ministry, a position perhaps even more difficult than finance minister," he said at a news conference marking his appointment in parliament earlier in the day.
"The one fortunate aspect of this is that we have set August 15 as the date to complete the work. I hope we keep to this timetable and that I can devote my full attention to the ministry," he said.
The committee is working to find a compromise to controverisal legislation that would enshrine in law Orthodox rabbis' long-standing monopoly on religious conversions to Judaism.
The legislation won preliminary approval from parliament in April but has caused an uproar in the influential Jewish community in the United States and is being challenged by non-Orthodox Jews.
As finance minister, Neeman faces a difficult agenda left by his predecessor, Dan Meridor, who resigned on June 18 after a dispute with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The Treasury is in the midst of preparing a new round of budget cuts at a time when newspaper reports say Netanyahu has promised new spending to keep the loyalty of his foreign minister, David Levy.

The economy is in a period of uncertainty, after changes in the exchange rate mechanism were announced June 18 and the Bank of Israel slashed interest rates. The shekel fell sharply in response and has since traded nervously.
Neeman said he expected full cooperation with the prime minister's office and the central bank.

"I am confident there will be complete cooperation with the prime minister's office," he said. "It's no secret that I came at the request of the prime minister. I come from the private sector and a professional. I am not a party man."
Neeman, a corporate attorney and former Treasury director-general, is active politically but unusually for an Israeli cabinet minister has not held elected office.
Meridor's term was characterised by political infighting with Netanyahu and tensions with the central bank over monetary and fiscal policy.

Neeman would not comment on his views regarding the budget or monetary policy, saying he was still studying the issues. He said he would begin holding working meetings with senior Treasury officials on Thursday.
